muscle:biceps#0.title: Where does the shoulder leave the biceps?
muscle:biceps#0.why: The section's payoff is being able to predict any curl's difficulty curve from shoulder position alone. Sorting real positions forces the reader to apply the rule instead of reading it.

spec.prompt: The elbow job is the same in all five. Which shoulder positions leave the biceps long and working hard, and which slide it toward active insufficiency?

items.label: Arm reached behind you
items.why: Shoulder extended, so the biceps is stretched at its shoulder end; the curl feels stronger

items.label: Incline dumbbell curl
items.why: Lying back drops the shoulder into extension, pre-stretching the long head

items.label: Preacher curl, bottom
items.why: Flexed shoulder plus extended elbow leaves the muscle long, but at poor leverage

items.label: Arm raised forward
items.why: Shoulder flexed, so the muscle is partly used up with little shortening range left

items.label: Preacher curl, top
items.why: Flexed shoulder plus flexing elbow, so it feels easy near the top

muscle:biceps#1.title: Bent arm vs. straight arm: who does the twisting
muscle:biceps#1.why: The paragraph welds four ideas together — angle-dependence, a second muscle, the mechanic, the screwdriver test. One row each pulls them apart and makes the bent-arm instinct obvious.

muscle:biceps#2.title: Same weight, three grips: who actually lifts it
muscle:biceps#2.why: The section stacks two separate mechanisms — tendon leverage and team substitution — onto three grips. Laid side by side, the reader can see that grip is a routing switch, not a variation.

muscle:biceps#3.title: The long head's route: from above the socket to the groove
muscle:biceps#3.why: The section's whole point is that an unusual anatomical path creates a mechanical problem. Reading the route as prose is hard to hold; laying it out as an ordered journey makes the friction — and therefore the front-of-shoulder pain — follow visibly from the anatomy.

steps.label: Supraglenoid tubercle
steps.sub: origin above the socket, off the labrum

steps.label: Inside the joint capsule
steps.sub: arches over the top of the humeral head

steps.label: Bicipital groove
steps.sub: exits through a tight bony canyon

steps.label: Under a ligament roof
steps.sub: transverse humeral ligament plus a cuff sling

steps.label: Slides on every movement
steps.sub: constant friction and shear

spec.outcome: Classic tendinopathy site: ache at the FRONT of the shoulder, often blamed on the cuff

muscle:biceps#4.title: Two biceps ruptures, opposite urgency — which sign belongs to which?
muscle:biceps#4.why: This is the section's central distinction and the one with real stakes: a proximal long-head tear is largely cosmetic and often left alone, while a distal tear has no backup and a roughly 2-3 week repair window. Making the reader place each sign forces the discrimination the prose only describes.

spec.prompt: Same muscle, two tear sites. Which findings belong to the proximal long-head rupture, and which to the distal one?

items.label: Popeye bulge, lower arm
items.why: freed at the top, the belly balls up DOWN the arm

items.label: Only 10-20% strength lost
items.why: the short head and brachialis still do the job

items.label: Older, degenerated tendon
items.why: snaps in its groove, sometimes with an audible pop

items.label: Often left untreated
items.why: largely a cosmetic and comfort issue; redundancy saves the arm

items.label: Reverse Popeye
items.why: the muscle balls up HIGHER on the arm

items.label: Hook test finds nothing
items.why: the fingertip sweeps through empty air; the taut tendon is gone

items.label: Catching a falling object
items.why: sudden eccentric overload, forearm forced straight against a hard contraction

items.label: Repair within 2-3 weeks
items.why: retracted tendon scars down; unrepaired costs ~30% flexion, ~40-50% supination

muscle:biceps#5.title: Three muscles, one job: who actually flexes your elbow
muscle:biceps#5.why: The section's argument is that the biceps is not the strongest elbow flexor and that grip position decides who leads. Side-by-side attributes make the division of labour — and why supinated-only curls train a third of the group — legible at a glance.

rows.attr: What it does to the look
values: Pushes the peak up and out

muscle:biceps#6.title: Shape or fibre mix? Attribute each fact
muscle:biceps#6.why: The section stacks two separate explanations — architecture and fibre type — and readers blur them. Sorting the consequences back to their cause forces the split to stick.

spec.prompt: Every fact below is true of the biceps. Does it follow from how its fibres are ARRANGED, or from what KIND of fibres they are?

items.label: Large, fast range
items.why: Long fibres in line with the tendon let it shorten a lot

items.label: Less force per size
items.why: Fusiform packs fewer fibres side by side than a pennate muscle

items.label: Sits on the brachialis
items.why: A range-and-speed muscle riding on top of a force muscle

items.label: Rewards heavy 5-8 sets
items.why: Heavier low-rep work recruits the high-threshold Type II fibres

items.label: Grows from pump work
items.why: Moderate-rep, higher-volume work fatigues and recruits those fibres another way

items.label: Fatigue-resistant carrying
items.why: Roughly 40% Type I fibres handle posture and carrying

muscle:biceps#7.title: Chin-up vs pull-up vs curl, on the same bar
muscle:biceps#7.why: The section's claim is that grip and load — not the exercise's label — decide which muscle works. Laying the three side by side makes the pull-up column the proof: same body, same bar, opposite bias.

muscle:biceps#8.title: One eccentric force, two destinations
muscle:biceps#8.why: The section's whole point is that growth and rupture share a mechanism and are separated only by control and progression. Sorting real scenarios makes the reader apply that line rather than read it.

spec.prompt: Lowering under load is the one event behind soreness, growth and tears. Which side of it does each belong to?

items.label: Slow controlled negative
items.why: High tension while lengthening: microdamage, then repair and reinforce

items.label: Stretch at the bottom
items.why: Tension in the lengthened position is the master growth signal

items.label: DOMS at 24-72 hours
items.why: The same eccentric microdamage that drives the hypertrophy response

items.label: Built up over time
items.why: Heavy eccentrics done slowly and progressively raise tendon tolerance

items.label: Catching a heavy load
items.why: Sudden unbraced overload forces the elbow open mid-contraction

items.label: A deadlift slipping
items.why: Unexpected maximal eccentric: the distal tendon is one rope, no backup

items.label: Arm-wrestling
items.why: Elbow forced to extend against a maximally contracting biceps

muscle:biceps#9.title: Two attachments, and what the second one lies on top of
muscle:biceps#9.why: The section is spatial and the prose fights it: a flat fan peels off the distal tendon, runs the OTHER way from the bone insertion, and forms a roof over the brachial artery and median nerve. Seeing the tendon split into a bone arm and a fascia arm — with the artery and nerve underneath the fan — is what makes both the load-sharing answer and the missed-rupture trap obvious in one look.

hotspots.label: Biceps muscle belly
hotspots.note: One muscle, two distal attachments — bone and fascia

hotspots.label: Distal tendon
hotspots.note: The aponeurosis peels off this tendon as a sheet

hotspots.label: Radial tuberosity
hotspots.note: The textbook bone insertion; bears concentrated force

hotspots.label: Bicipital aponeurosis
hotspots.note: Flat fan blending into ulnar-side forearm flexor fascia

hotspots.label: Artery and nerve
hotspots.note: Brachial artery, median nerve — roofed by the fan

hotspots.label: Tether in rupture
hotspots.note: Intact fan stops the torn muscle retracting — masks it

muscle:biceps#10.title: The tendon tap, step by step — and why no brain is involved
muscle:biceps#10.why: The reflex is described in one long sentence that a reader skims as 'tap, jerk'. Broken into its links, it becomes visible that the loop goes muscle → cord → muscle and never reaches the brain, which is exactly why it is fast, involuntary, and diagnostic: each link is a place the loop can break, so an absent jerk indicts C5–C6 or the musculocutaneous nerve rather than the biceps.

steps.label: Hammer taps tendon
steps.sub: clinician strikes the biceps tendon

steps.label: Muscle suddenly stretched
steps.sub: the tap is a fast stretch, not a load

steps.label: Muscle spindles fire
steps.sub: stretch receptors inside the muscle

steps.label: Sensory nerve to cord
steps.sub: signal travels up to the C5–C6 level

steps.label: Straight back down
steps.sub: motor nerve — no brain required

steps.label: Biceps contracts
steps.sub: the forearm jerks, involuntarily

spec.outcome: An absent or weak jerk points at C5–C6 or the musculocutaneous nerve — not at the muscle.

muscle:biceps#fundamentals.title: Anchored end, moving end, or neither?
muscle:biceps#fundamentals.why: The section's whole payoff is that BOTH origins sit on the scapula and the insertion sits past the elbow — which is why the muscle crosses two joints. Making the reader place each landmark forces that conclusion instead of stating it.

spec.prompt: The biceps can only shorten and pull between an anchored ORIGIN and a moving INSERTION. Place each landmark.

items.label: Supraglenoid tubercle
items.why: Long head starts here, a bump just above the shoulder socket

items.label: Coracoid process
items.why: Short head starts on this hook at the front of the scapula

items.label: Radial tuberosity
items.why: Knob on the radius just past the elbow; the main insertion

items.label: Bicipital aponeurosis
items.why: Flat sheet fanning off into the forearm's connective-tissue wrapping

items.label: Bony groove in humerus
items.why: Long head's tendon only runs down it — no head attaches to the humerus

items.label: Musculocutaneous nerve
items.why: Not an attachment — it delivers the C5–C6 signal that fires the muscle

muscle:biceps#analogy.title: The rope and the spool, drawn
muscle:biceps#analogy.why: The prose ends with 'keep the image' and then supplies no image. This is that image, pinned onto the real arm so rope=biceps, spool=radius, and the two jobs (bend, spin) are visible at the places they happen.

hotspots.label: The rope
hotspots.note: The biceps and its tendon — one thing that can only shorten and pull

hotspots.label: Pull, elbow bends
hotspots.note: Job one: the whole forearm swings up toward you — elbow flexion

hotspots.label: The spool
hotspots.note: The radius, the forearm bone on the thumb side, free to spin

hotspots.label: Glued far side

hotspots.label: Spin, palm up
hotspots.note: Job two: the spool's face turns to the ceiling — supination

hotspots.label: Palm down un-wraps
hotspots.note: Pronation partly unwinds the rope, costing spin and pull; brachialis takes over

muscle:biceps#expertLens.title: The four questions a specialist actually asks
muscle:biceps#expertLens.why: The section is explicitly four lenses, but they arrive as one paragraph so they read as one blur. Laid side by side against the same three questions — what it asks, what the clue is, what it changes — the reader can see that each lens is a different decision, not more description.

pathway:gaba-glutamate#0.title: Is it the channel, or does it phone the channel?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#0.why: The section's whole payoff is one split — ionotropic receptors ARE the pore, metabotropic ones are GPCRs that start a slow cascade. A reader who can place all six named receptor families on the correct side has actually got it; reading the paragraph twice does not prove that.

spec.prompt: Sort each receptor: is it the ion channel itself, or a GPCR that acts through a cascade?

items.label: AMPA
items.why: Pore opens instantly; fast Na+ in = instant push

items.label: NMDA
items.why: Ionotropic; passes Ca2+, the coincidence-detecting learning switch

items.label: Kainate
items.why: Glutamate's third ionotropic receptor, a modulatory cousin

items.label: mGluR1-8
items.why: Glutamate's metabotropic set; tunes gain up or down

items.label: GABA-A
items.why: The chloride pore itself; fast Cl- = instant brake

items.label: GABA-B
items.why: GPCR: opens K+, closes Ca2+; slow lingering brake

pathway:gaba-glutamate#1.title: Four ways to press the same brake — and why one of them kills
pathway:gaba-glutamate#1.why: This section is a four-item bullet list where single items run 40-143 words, but it is really one comparison table: same receptor, different pocket, different effect on the opening, different ceiling. Laid out as a grid, the frequency-vs-duration / ceiling-vs-no-ceiling contrast the prose calls 'the most important safety concept in all of sedative pharmacology' becomes a single glance instead of a 470-word read.

values: Section does not name the site
The body's own PAM, like benzos
No - a PAM, needs GABA already present
Yes, at high dose it prises the channel open
No - a PAM, so GABA must be there
Ceiling; rarely kills alone, but co-ingestion does
NO ceiling; kills by respiratory arrest
Endogenous dial: cycle shifts mood, seizure threshold
General anesthesia = forcibly maximizing the brake

pathway:gaba-glutamate#2.title: The AND-gate, in order: what has to be true before NMDA opens
pathway:gaba-glutamate#2.why: The 375-word list buries the section's headline claim — that NMDA is a coincidence detector — inside item 1. Laying the gating conditions out as an ordered chain makes visible that AMPA has to fire FIRST, that glutamate alone is inert, and that the co-agonist is a third simultaneous requirement, not an afterthought.

steps.label: Glutamate binds AMPA
steps.sub: plain Na+ enters, membrane depolarises

steps.label: Glutamate binds NMDA
steps.sub: alone this does nothing — the Mg2+ stays

steps.label: Glycine or D-serine bound
steps.sub: required co-agonist, at a separate site

steps.label: Depolarisation ejects Mg2+
steps.sub: the resting-voltage pore plug pops out

steps.label: NMDA opens to Ca2+
steps.sub: Ca2+ instructs; it doesn't just excite

steps.label: CaMKII inserts AMPA receptors
steps.sub: the synapse is strengthened

spec.outcome: LTP. Both 'input arrived' and 'cell was already active' had to be true at once.

pathway:gaba-glutamate#3.title: Clearance is a control point — so which way does each of these push glutamate?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#3.why: The section's central claim is that glutamate is never destroyed, only cleared, which makes every step of the clearance loop druggable. Sorting a drug, a toxin, a metabolic state and a supplement into the same two buckets forces the reader to apply that claim rather than nod at it — and the glutamine item lands the section's own closing warning.

spec.prompt: Glutamate is never destroyed at the synapse — only cleared. Which of these speed clearance up, and which leave glutamate lingering?

items.label: Ceftriaxone
items.why: an antibiotic that upregulates GLT-1, the main clearance transporter

items.label: Riluzole
items.why: reduces glutamate release; proposed also to boost EAAT2

items.label: Boosting EAAT2 expression
items.why: an active drug-discovery target for exactly this reason

items.label: Ischemia
items.why: clearance costs ATP, so metabolic failure IS excitotoxicity

items.label: Toxins slowing EAAT2
items.why: transporter stalls, glutamate lingers, system pushed toward excitotoxicity

items.label: Extra glutamine supply
items.why: the precursor neurons reconvert with glutaminase — not innocent 'fuel'

pathway:gaba-glutamate#4.title: Same channel, three chloride states, three opposite answers
pathway:gaba-glutamate#4.why: The section's whole argument is that one identical GABA-A opening produces inhibition, excitation, or a failing brake depending only on which pump is winning. Laid side by side, the reader can read the pump row and predict the outcome row without being told.

pathway:gaba-glutamate#5.title: Which control point does each calming compound actually grab?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#5.why: The section's payoff is that 'calming' does not mean 'GABA'. Forcing the reader to place each compound before the reveal exposes the assumption — and the answer key shows only one of the seven is a straightforward GABA-A grab, while four work entirely on the accelerator.

spec.prompt: Everything here calms. But which side of the map does each one actually grab — the GABA brake, the glutamate accelerator, or both?

items.label: Apigenin (chamomile)
items.why: Weak ligand at GABA-A's benzodiazepine site — a feather-light PAM.

items.label: L-theanine
items.why: Weakly blocks glutamate receptors and starves glutamate synthesis of glutamine.

items.label: Magnesium
items.why: Mg2+ is the ion plugging the NMDA pore. Accelerator, not GABA.

items.label: Gabapentin / pregabalin
items.why: Binds α2δ calcium subunit, cutting glutamate release. Never touches GABA.

items.label: Ketamine
items.why: NMDA antagonist — blocks inhibitory interneurons, causing a glutamate surge.

items.label: Alcohol
items.why: Potentiates GABA-A and blocks NMDA — brake and accelerator together.

items.label: Glycine
items.why: Own Cl− channel brake; also NMDA co-agonist. Sleep via temperature.

pathway:gaba-glutamate#6.title: Which 'GABA' drugs actually raise GABA?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#6.why: The section's entire argument is that a drug's name is a historical artifact of the chemists' intent, not its mechanism. Making the reader commit to an answer before the reveal is the only way that lands.

spec.prompt: Sort each one by whether it actually raises GABA in the brain.

items.label: Gabapentin
items.why: Binds the alpha-2-delta calcium subunit; cuts glutamate release instead

items.label: Pregabalin
items.why: Same alpha-2-delta target; turns down the accelerator, not up the brake

items.label: Vigabatrin
items.why: Irreversibly blocks GABA-transaminase, the degrading enzyme, so GABA accumulates

items.label: Tiagabine
items.why: Blocks the GAT-1 reuptake transporter, so released GABA lingers in the synapse

items.label: Valproate
items.why: Multiple actions, including raising GABA

items.label: GABA supplement
items.why: Crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly; any effect is likely gut or vagal

items.label: Caffeine
items.why: Blocks adenosine receptors; disinhibits and raises net excitation instead

pathway:gaba-glutamate#7.title: One axis, read at different volumes
pathway:gaba-glutamate#7.why: The section's claim is that a single ratio runs through neurology, psychiatry and addiction medicine. Placing the conditions on one axis shows the tilt has a direction: schizophrenia sits on the opposite side from seizure, which is exactly why NMDA blockers mimic psychosis rather than treating it.

items.label: Schizophrenia
items.note: NMDA hypofunction; ketamine and PCP transiently mimic it

items.label: Autism
items.note: altered balance in specific circuits; direction not settled

items.label: Anxiety, insomnia
items.note: mild chronic tilt; why GABA-A PAMs treat both

items.label: Benzo withdrawal
items.note: GABA-A downregulated, so too few brakes remain

items.label: Seizure
items.note: self-recruiting glutamatergic chain reaction across whole regions

items.label: Stroke, TBI
items.note: excitotoxicity and calcium overload kill the neurons

pathway:gaba-glutamate#8.title: The four clocks running at once
pathway:gaba-glutamate#8.why: The section says confusing the timescales is the single most common error in reasoning about a drug. A scale would show the span but not the mix-up; laying machinery, function and example side by side makes 'I feel calm now' and 'my system is healthier' visibly different rows of the same table.

values: A night's study; one ketamine dose

pathway:gaba-glutamate#fundamentals.title: Which ion, which direction, therefore which sign?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#fundamentals.why: The section ends by telling the reader that this one question is 'the whole game'. A sort makes them actually run it instead of nodding at it.

spec.prompt: Each move below happens at a synapse. Does it push the neuron toward firing, or away from it?

items.label: Na+ flows in
items.why: positive charge enters — inside gets more positive, closer to threshold

items.label: Ca2+ flows in
items.why: also a positive ion entering — voltage rises toward the ~−55 mV threshold

items.label: Cl− flows in
items.why: negative charge enters — inside gets more negative, further from firing

items.label: K+ flows out
items.why: positive charge leaves — inside gets more negative, further from firing

items.label: Glutamate binds
items.why: it opens Na+/Ca2+ channels — the accelerator

items.label: GABA binds
items.why: it opens Cl− channels — the brake

pathway:gaba-glutamate#analogy.title: Three ways a foot meets the brake pedal
pathway:gaba-glutamate#analogy.why: The analogy is not one image but three variants of the same pedal, and the difference between them is the whole safety lesson. Laid side by side, gentle-vs-slammed-vs-reversed separates cleanly; read as prose it blurs.

values: presses the pedal to the floor by itself
not a pedal problem; the cable is reversed

no — the car moves forward instead
it acts alone, with no ceiling from traffic
the pump that charges the brakes isn't installed yet

pathway:gaba-glutamate#expertLens.title: The pharmacologist's five-question routine
pathway:gaba-glutamate#expertLens.why: The section's claim is that these five questions, run in order, replace memorising drugs. Rendered as an ordered chain with its payoff at the end, the routine becomes something the reader can reuse on a molecule the lesson never mentions.

steps.label: Which control point?
steps.sub: synthesis · release · receptor · clearance · gradient pump

steps.label: Agonist, antagonist, modulator?
steps.sub: modulator needs the transmitter present → sets the safety ceiling

steps.label: Which ion, which sign?
steps.sub: voltage up or voltage down

steps.label: Which timescale?
steps.sub: fast lid · slow tone · rewrite · homeostatic reset

steps.sub: days-to-weeks pushback → tolerance, dependence, withdrawal

pathway:gaba-glutamate#mechSteps.title: Every control point — which way does each one tip?
pathway:gaba-glutamate#mechSteps.why: Step 8's predict prompt asks the reader to list every point in steps 1-8 where a molecule could grab the system, and step 9 grades them with six named levers. Right now that payoff is a prose instruction with no way to check the answer. This turns it into the actual test: eight levers pulled from eight different steps, each one classified brake-ward or accelerator-ward. It forces a pass across the whole cascade rather than step-by-step reading, and it makes the section's real claim visible — the same nine steps read as one control panel.

spec.prompt: A molecule grabs each lever below. Which way does the E/I balance tip?

items.label: Block presynaptic Ca2+ channels
items.why: Step 2: the control point gabapentin grabs — less calcium, less glutamate spilled.

items.label: Boost GAD enzyme activity
items.why: Step 6: GAD snips glutamate into GABA — more GAD, more brake fluid.

items.label: Make GABA-A more responsive
items.why: Step 9: same GABA, bigger chloride response — one of the six listed levers.

items.label: Block the NMDA receptor
items.why: Step 9: blocking the glutamate receptor is listed as a calming lever.

items.label: Deplete vitamin B6
items.why: Step 6: B6 is GAD's cofactor — isoniazid depletes it and can trigger seizures.

items.label: Block EAAT2 glutamate clearance
items.why: Step 5: glutamate lingers, Ca2+ floods the cell — excitotoxicity.

items.label: Lose the KCC2 pump
items.why: Step 8: internal Cl- rises, so GABA weakens or even excites.

items.label: Park more AMPA receptors
items.why: Step 3: AMPA number is synaptic strength — more receptors, more fast excitation.
